title: Why so many names
hookLine: a thousand names say that no single name can hold Him

lines: A NAME ON FORMS, A NAME FOR FRIENDS.
NO ONE NAME IS THE WHOLE PERSON.
cards: How many names do you have? Your full name on forms. A shorter one for friends.
Something only your grandmother called you. Mom, or Dad, or Auntie, to someone. A nickname from a soccer team you'd rather forget.
Each one is true, each holds a different piece of you, and not one of them is the whole person. So what happens when the one being named is infinitely larger than any person?

teach.h: HUNDREDS OF NAMES IN ONE HYMN.
teach.b: Over the last four weeks you've heard a tiny slice of Jaap's names. Timeless. Merciful.
Sun of suns. Lamp of beauty. Provider.
Hundreds more are still waiting. Why so many? Jaap answered in its first stanza: who can tell all Your names?
The wise speak the names drawn from Your deeds.

teach.h: NO LIST CAN FINISH THE JOB.
teach.b: So the long list isn't trying to finish the job. It admits the job can't be finished, and praises anyway. Each name is a window into one room of a house too big to see at once.

Guru Nanak said the same in the nineteenth pauri of Japji: countless are Your names, countless Your places. Then he adds that even the word countless is too heavy to carry. Notice where the names come from, too.

The Guru Granth Sahib calls the One by names from many places: Ram, Hari and Gobind, which Hindus also use; Allah, Khuda and Rahim, which Muslims also use; and Waheguru, the name that became the Sikh word of wonder.
Jaap adds Sanskrit, Persian and Arabic names of its own. Sikhs don't treat any one of these as the password. The One, Sikh teaching holds, is beyond them all, and present in each.
It's like the stars: the more you look, the more there are.

how: Sikhs call the One by many names in prayer and kirtan, Waheguru, Akal Purakh, Ram, Hari, Gobind, Kartar and more, following the Guru Granth Sahib, which uses names from many languages.

o: countless names, more than any list can hold
a secret name only the Guru may speak
the hundred names a child learns by heart

games.q: why so many names — tap the pairs.
p: who can tell all Your names?
one window into a vast house

s: Jaap's long list tries to name everything about the One
it admits the job can't be finished, and praises anyway.
the Guru Granth Sahib uses names like Ram, Hari, Allah and Rahim
names from many places, with the One beyond them all.
Guru Nanak says even the word countless is too heavy to carry

games.q: you want to praise the One, and you've found a name you love. why does Jaap keep adding hundreds more?
o: because the first ones were wrong.
because no single name can hold the One.
to make the hymn longer than others.
games.why: each name is a window into one room of a house too big to see at once; the list can never be finished.

practice: Write three names for the Divine: ones you've learned here, like Akal or Kripaal, ones from your own background, or deed-names from your own life, like the one who carried me last winter.
If the word Divine doesn't fit you, write three names for whatever you feel grateful toward. Read them slowly, and notice that each one opens a different window.

wordCard.voice: Asankh naav, countless names. No single name can hold the One: Jaap's hundreds of names admit the list can never be finished, and praise anyway.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: asankh naav, countless names, from Japji's nineteenth pauri.

carryVoice: Your line: more names than stars. Nobody has ever counted either of them. See you tomorrow.
